07-rates-of-reaction.explain: The scheme wanted the proportion idea (more collisions exceed the activation energy) as its own point, distinct from collision frequency. Merging them lost a mark.

07-rates-of-reaction.q: To compare two catalysts fairly using time-to-collect-20 cm³, the better catalyst gives…
07-rates-of-reaction.explain: Less time for the same job = faster rate: rate ∝ 1/time. With time-based measurements the comparison flips — shorter wins.

07-rates-of-reaction.q: Which is NOT a way of following the rate of a reaction that makes a gas?
options: Volume collected in a gas syringe
Time for a fixed volume to form
Measuring the colour of the flask
07-rates-of-reaction.explain: The school's three methods are mass loss, gas volume, and timing. Colour only works for reactions with a colour change.

07-rates-of-reaction.q: On a volume–time graph, the reaction is fastest where the curve is…
07-rates-of-reaction.explain: Gradient = rate. Steepest (the start) = fastest; flat = finished.

07-rates-of-reaction.q: The reaction is complete when the volume–time curve…
07-rates-of-reaction.explain: A level curve means no more product is forming — a reactant has run out.

07-rates-of-reaction.q: Doubling the concentration of acid (all else equal) makes the initial rate roughly…
07-rates-of-reaction.explain: Twice the particles per volume → about twice the collision frequency → about twice the rate.

07-rates-of-reaction.q: A gas-pressure increase speeds up a gas reaction because…
options: the same particles are squeezed into less volume, colliding more often
07-rates-of-reaction.explain: Pressure for gases is what concentration is for solutions — more crowding, more frequent collisions. No energy change.

07-rates-of-reaction.q: The final volume of gas produced depends on…
07-rates-of-reaction.explain: Rate factors change how FAST the plateau is reached, never its height — only the amounts change how MUCH.

07-rates-of-reaction.q: In the H₂O₂ practical, the same volume and concentration of peroxide is used in every run so that…
options: the comparison of catalysts is valid
07-rates-of-reaction.explain: Change only the catalyst; control everything else. Naming the controlled variables is what scores — 'fair test' alone does not.

07-rates-of-reaction.q: A tangent drawn to a curve at t = 4 min should…
options: touch the curve at 4 min only
07-rates-of-reaction.explain: One touch-point at the stated time — then a large triangle for the gradient.

07-rates-of-reaction.q: Rate = 24 cm³ ÷ 8 min from a tangent triangle gives…
07-rates-of-reaction.explain: Δy ÷ Δx = 24 ÷ 8 = 3, units cm³/min — the y-unit over the x-unit, always.

07-rates-of-reaction.q: The average rate over an experiment lasting 80 s that made 88 cm³ of gas is…
07-rates-of-reaction.explain: 88 ÷ 80 = 1.1 cm³/s — fine for an AVERAGE; a rate AT a time still needs the tangent.

07-rates-of-reaction.q: Increasing the temperature by 10 °C typically…
07-rates-of-reaction.explain: The proportion of collisions beating the activation energy climbs steeply — the dominant effect of temperature.

07-rates-of-reaction.q: The 2024 scheme capped at 1 mark any concentration answer that mentioned…
07-rates-of-reaction.explain: Energy language belongs only in temperature answers. Concentration = crowding → frequency, nothing else.

07-rates-of-reaction.q: A catalyst's mass at the end of a reaction is…
options: the same as at the start
07-rates-of-reaction.explain: Chemically unchanged and recoverable — filter, dry, reweigh: identical.

07-rates-of-reaction.q: On an energy-level diagram, a catalyst changes…
options: the height of the activation-energy barrier
07-rates-of-reaction.explain: Only the barrier drops (via the alternative pathway); start and end energies — and the overall energy change — are untouched.

07-rates-of-reaction.q: Which change increases the rate WITHOUT changing the final amount of product?
options: Using powder instead of chips (same mass)
07-rates-of-reaction.explain: Surface area is pure rate: same moles, same plateau, reached sooner. More reactant changes the amount.

07-rates-of-reaction.q: In the marble-chip experiment the balance reading falls because…
options: carbon dioxide escapes through the cotton wool
07-rates-of-reaction.explain: The mass loss IS the CO₂ leaving — the reason this set-up measures rate at all.

07-rates-of-reaction.q: The steeper start of the powdered-marble curve compared with chips shows…
07-rates-of-reaction.explain: Gradient = rate. Same plateau, steeper approach — the surface-area signature.

07-rates-of-reaction.q: "More successful collisions per unit time" — the phrase 'per unit time' matters because…
options: rate is about frequency, and 2025's M3 was refused without a time link
07-rates-of-reaction.explain: The teacher commentary is explicit: no time reference, no mark. Frequency is collisions PER SECOND, not just 'more'.

07-rates-of-reaction.q: Which experiment best investigates surface area?
options: Same mass of marble as chips vs powder, same acid
Different acids with the same marble
07-rates-of-reaction.explain: One variable: particle size. Same mass, same acid volume/concentration, same temperature — spec practical 3.15.

07-rates-of-reaction.q: The units g/s would be read from a graph of…
07-rates-of-reaction.explain: Rate units = y-axis unit per x-axis unit. Mass-loss experiments give g/s; gas-syringe ones give cm³/s or cm³/min.

07-rates-of-reaction.q: Why does a reaction slow down long before it stops?
options: Reactant concentration falls as it is used up, so collisions become less frequent
07-rates-of-reaction.explain: The curve's whole shape is falling concentration: fewer reactant particles → rarer collisions → shallower gradient.

07-rates-of-reaction.q: Two identical experiments differ only in acid volume: 50 cm³ vs 100 cm³ of the SAME concentration, with marble in excess. The 100 cm³ run…
options: levels off at twice the gas volume
levels off at the same volume
07-rates-of-reaction.explain: Same concentration = same initial rate; twice the acid = twice the moles = twice the product. Rate factors vs amount factors, cleanly split.

07-rates-of-reaction.q: MnO₂ in the H₂O₂ decomposition can be shown to be a catalyst (not a reactant) because…
options: it is recovered unchanged in mass and still works
07-rates-of-reaction.explain: Recoverable, unchanged, reusable — and absent from the overall equation 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂.

07-rates-of-reaction.q: The graph mark "single smooth curve" was lost in 2023 by students who…
07-rates-of-reaction.explain: The commentary named blunt pencils and feathery lines. One clean line, drawn once.

07-rates-of-reaction.q: In a clock-style experiment, a FASTER reaction gives…
07-rates-of-reaction.explain: Rate and time are inverse: rate ∝ 1/time. Shorter time to the fixed endpoint = faster.

07-rates-of-reaction.q: Raising temperature affects which TWO things about collisions?
options: Both their frequency and their energy
07-rates-of-reaction.explain: Hotter particles collide more often AND harder — and the energy part (more beating the activation energy) is the bigger effect.

07-rates-of-reaction.q: The activation energy of a reaction is changed by…
07-rates-of-reaction.explain: Only a catalyst changes the barrier. Temperature changes how many collisions CLEAR the unchanged barrier.

07-rates-of-reaction.q: A student says 'the particles have more chance to collide'. The scheme's problem with this is…
options: chance is not frequency — collisions per unit time must be stated
07-rates-of-reaction.explain: "IGNORE greater chance of collision" is written on the 2021 scheme. Frequency, per unit time — the exact words.

07-rates-of-reaction.q: Cooling a reaction mixture makes the rate…
07-rates-of-reaction.explain: Less energy, fewer successful collisions, lower frequency — every temperature effect in reverse.

07-rates-of-reaction.q: The correct pairing of practical and measurement is…
options: marble + acid → mass loss on a balance; H₂O₂ → gas syringe
07-rates-of-reaction.explain: The two named practicals as the school runs them: CO₂ escaping is weighed; O₂ is collected. (Either method can work — this is how the papers show them.)

07-rates-of-reaction.q: Why is only a SMALL mass of catalyst needed?
options: It is not used up, so each particle keeps working
07-rates-of-reaction.explain: Unchanged at the end means endlessly reusable during the reaction — a little goes forever.

07-rates-of-reaction.q: Rate of reaction is best defined as…
options: the total amount of product formed
the amount of reactant used or product formed per unit time
the time taken for a reaction
07-rates-of-reaction.explain: Per unit time is the whole idea. Total amount is a different question — rate factors change speed, not yield.

07-rates-of-reaction.q: Which change would NOT increase the rate of a reaction between marble chips and acid?
options: Using a larger volume of the same acid
07-rates-of-reaction.explain: More acid of the SAME concentration means more product eventually, but the collision frequency at the start is unchanged. Amount ≠ rate.

07-rates-of-reaction.q: For particles to react they must collide…
options: with energy at or above the activation energy
07-rates-of-reaction.explain: That energy threshold is the definition of a SUCCESSFUL collision — and the word 'successful' carries its own mark.

07-rates-of-reaction.q: On a mass-loss graph for marble chips and acid, the line becomes horizontal when…
options: one reactant is completely used up
07-rates-of-reaction.explain: No more gas is escaping because the reaction has finished — the limiting reactant is gone.

07-rates-of-reaction.q: Which measurement would you take to follow a reaction that produces a gas?
options: Volume of gas in a syringe or mass lost on a balance
The mass of the flask before the reaction only
07-rates-of-reaction.explain: The two standard set-ups. A single before-reading tells you nothing about rate — you need readings over time.

07-rates-of-reaction.q: A catalyst does NOT…
options: get used up in the reaction
07-rates-of-reaction.explain: It is chemically unchanged at the end and can be recovered and reused. Everything else listed is exactly what it does.

07-rates-of-reaction.q: Increasing the surface area of a solid reactant increases the rate because…
options: more particles are exposed for collisions
07-rates-of-reaction.explain: More exposed surface → more frequent collisions. No energy language belongs in a surface-area answer.

07-rates-of-reaction.q: Two runs use the same mass of marble but different chip sizes. Compared with the chips, the powder's graph…
options: is steeper and levels off at the same height
is steeper and levels off higher
is shallower and levels off lower
07-rates-of-reaction.explain: Same moles → same final volume; bigger surface area → faster start. Sketching that curve correctly is worth two marks most years.

07-rates-of-reaction.q: Which unit could NOT be a rate of reaction?
07-rates-of-reaction.explain: g/cm³ is density — no time in it. A rate always has a quantity divided by a TIME.

07-rates-of-reaction.q: Why does the rate fall as a reaction proceeds?
options: The reactants are used up, so collisions become less frequent
07-rates-of-reaction.explain: Falling concentration = fewer particles per volume = rarer collisions. That is the whole shape of the curve.

08-electrolysis-and-redox.q: Solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity because…
options: its ions are fixed in the lattice
08-electrolysis-and-redox.explain: The ions exist but cannot move. Electron-based answers score zero — ionic conduction is always about ions.

08-electrolysis-and-redox.q: During electrolysis, positive ions move to the…
08-electrolysis-and-redox.explain: Cations → cathode (negative electrode) → gain electrons = reduction. Anions → anode → lose electrons = oxidation.

08-electrolysis-and-redox.q: The correct half-equation for chlorine forming at the anode is…
08-electrolysis-and-redox.explain: Chlorine is diatomic and the electrons leave (oxidation, so they sit on the right). 2023's commentary: "fascinating variations including Cl⁺ and Cl₃" — all wrong.

08-electrolysis-and-redox.q: Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Mg is a reduction because…
08-electrolysis-and-redox.explain: The ION gains the electrons and becomes the metal. "Magnesium gains electrons" earned double exclamation marks from the 2023 marker — it is not true.

08-electrolysis-and-redox.q: Electrolysing concentrated sodium chloride SOLUTION gives, at the cathode…
08-electrolysis-and-redox.explain: Water supplies H⁺, and hydrogen is less reactive than sodium — so H₂ is discharged and Na⁺ stays in solution. Molten NaCl (no water) gives sodium.

08-electrolysis-and-redox.q: The solution near the cathode of NaCl(aq) electrolysis turns universal indicator…
options: blue/purple, because OH⁻ ions are left behind
08-electrolysis-and-redox.explain: Removing H⁺ leaves Na⁺ and OH⁻ — sodium hydroxide. 2025's "very badly done" question: name the colour AND the hydroxide ion.

08-electrolysis-and-redox.q: The correct half-equation for oxygen forming at the anode in a solution is…
08-electrolysis-and-redox.explain: Solutions contain no free O²⁻ ions — the oxygen comes from water (or 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻). 2O²⁻ was the year group's favourite wrong answer in 2023.

08-electrolysis-and-redox.q: Electrolysing copper(II) sulfate solution with inert electrodes leaves behind…
08-electrolysis-and-redox.explain: Cu²⁺ is removed as copper metal; H⁺ (from water) and SO₄²⁻ accumulate → dilute H₂SO₄, and the blue colour fades.

08-electrolysis-and-redox.q: Which is a suitable inert electrode material?
08-electrolysis-and-redox.explain: Graphite/carbon or platinum (gold and silver also accepted) — materials that carry current without reacting.

08-electrolysis-and-redox.q: The test for hydrogen gas is…
options: a lit splint gives a squeaky pop
08-electrolysis-and-redox.explain: LIT splint → pop = H₂. Glowing splint relighting is oxygen — 2024 rejected the swap. Limewater = CO₂; bleached litmus = chlorine.

08-electrolysis-and-redox.q: Electrolysis of NaCl(aq) collects less chlorine than hydrogen because…
options: some chlorine dissolves in the water
08-electrolysis-and-redox.explain: Equal moles are made, but chlorine is appreciably soluble — some never reaches the tube. Same reason oxygen under-collects in the water electrolysis.

08-electrolysis-and-redox.q: An oxidising agent is a substance that…
08-electrolysis-and-redox.explain: It takes electrons (or gives oxygen) — and is itself reduced. The reducing agent is its mirror: donates electrons / removes oxygen, and is itself oxidised.

08-electrolysis-and-redox.q: In 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻, the species oxidised is…
08-electrolysis-and-redox.explain: The bromide IONS lose the electrons. "Bromine loses electrons" was rejected in 2025 — bromine is the product, not the loser.

08-electrolysis-and-redox.q: Why is dilute acid added to water before electrolysing it?
08-electrolysis-and-redox.explain: Pure water barely conducts. The accepted wording is "increases the conductivity" — "helps carry the current" was ignored in 2021.

08-electrolysis-and-redox.q: Electrolysis of molten lead(II) bromide gives…
options: lead at the anode and bromine at the cathode
lead at the cathode and bromine at the anode
08-electrolysis-and-redox.explain: Molten compound, no water: the metal at the negative electrode (Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb), the non-metal at the positive (2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻).

08-electrolysis-and-redox.q: Electrolysis is…
options: breaking down a compound using electricity
08-electrolysis-and-redox.explain: Electric current in, decomposition out. Melting/dissolving just frees the ions so it can happen.

08-electrolysis-and-redox.q: The electrolyte must be molten or dissolved because…
options: the ions must be free to move
08-electrolysis-and-redox.explain: Moving ions ARE the current inside the electrolyte — locked ions, no electrolysis.

08-electrolysis-and-redox.q: An anion is…
options: a positive ion, attracted to the anode
a negative ion, attracted to the anode
a negative ion, attracted to the cathode
08-electrolysis-and-redox.explain: Anion = negative → anode (+). Cation = positive → cathode (−). Spec point 1.57C verbatim.

08-electrolysis-and-redox.q: At the cathode, the reaction is always…
08-electrolysis-and-redox.explain: Positive ions GAIN electrons there — reduction (OIL RIG: gain).

08-electrolysis-and-redox.q: The half-equation for copper depositing at the cathode is…
08-electrolysis-and-redox.explain: The copper ION gains two electrons. Electrons on the LEFT for reduction.

08-electrolysis-and-redox.q: Electrolysing molten sodium chloride gives, at the two electrodes…
08-electrolysis-and-redox.explain: No water, no competition: the compound's own elements — Na at the cathode, Cl₂ at the anode.

08-electrolysis-and-redox.q: Copper forms at the cathode of CuSO₄(aq) but hydrogen forms from K₂SO₄(aq) because…
options: copper is less reactive than hydrogen, potassium is more reactive
08-electrolysis-and-redox.explain: The LESS reactive of metal-vs-hydrogen is discharged. Cu below H → copper; K above H → hydrogen instead.

08-electrolysis-and-redox.q: The product at the anode when a halide solution is electrolysed is…
08-electrolysis-and-redox.explain: Halide present → halogen (Cl₂, Br₂). No halide (sulfate/nitrate) → oxygen from water.

08-electrolysis-and-redox.q: The gas at the anode of dilute sulfuric acid electrolysis is…
08-electrolysis-and-redox.explain: No halide → oxygen (2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻); hydrogen appears at the cathode. The Hofmann setup from 2025.

08-electrolysis-and-redox.q: In the Hofmann voltameter, the volume of hydrogen compared with oxygen is about…
08-electrolysis-and-redox.explain: Four electrons make 2H₂ but only 1O₂ — a 2:1 mole (and volume) ratio, slightly under for O₂ because some dissolves.

08-electrolysis-and-redox.q: Which is a correct statement of OIL RIG?
options: Reduction is loss of oxygen only
Oxidation is loss of electrons; reduction is gain
08-electrolysis-and-redox.explain: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain — of electrons. (The oxygen definitions run alongside for extraction chemistry.)

08-electrolysis-and-redox.q: In Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu, the zinc is…
options: oxidised — it loses electrons to become Zn²⁺
08-electrolysis-and-redox.explain: Zn atoms → Zn²⁺ (loss = oxidation); Cu²⁺ ions gain those electrons (reduction). Displacement IS redox.

08-electrolysis-and-redox.q: The purpose of the lamp/ammeter in an electrolysis circuit is to show…
08-electrolysis-and-redox.explain: A glowing lamp = charge moving = the electrolyte is conducting — the conduction test from 2023's Q2.

08-electrolysis-and-redox.q: Which solution, when electrolysed, leaves nitric acid behind?
08-electrolysis-and-redox.explain: Ag deposits (unreactive), O₂ leaves the anode, H⁺ + NO₃⁻ remain = HNO₃. KNO₃ loses only water (H₂ + O₂) and stays itself.

08-electrolysis-and-redox.q: The half-equation 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ shows…
08-electrolysis-and-redox.explain: Electrons on the right = loss = oxidation, at the positive electrode — the accepted alternative to the water version.

08-electrolysis-and-redox.q: Aluminium is manufactured by electrolysis of…
08-electrolysis-and-redox.explain: MOLTEN oxide — from a solution, hydrogen would form instead of the metal (Al is far above hydrogen).

08-electrolysis-and-redox.q: Why does the blue colour fade during CuSO₄(aq) electrolysis with inert electrodes?
options: Cu²⁺ ions (the blue) are removed as copper deposits
08-electrolysis-and-redox.explain: The colour IS the copper ion; plating it out drains the blue and leaves sulfuric acid.

08-electrolysis-and-redox.q: The observation at an electrode making a gas is…
08-electrolysis-and-redox.explain: Say what you see. Naming the gas is a conclusion — the schemes IGNORE it as an observation.

08-electrolysis-and-redox.q: Chlorine gas can be identified because it…
08-electrolysis-and-redox.explain: Bleached litmus = chlorine. Pop = H₂, relight = O₂, milky = CO₂ — four tests, keep them straight.

08-electrolysis-and-redox.q: An electrode that does not react with the electrolyte or products is called…
08-electrolysis-and-redox.explain: Inert = chemically uninvolved: platinum or graphite/carbon.

08-electrolysis-and-redox.q: In the electrolysis of molten PbBr₂, the observation at the anode is…
08-electrolysis-and-redox.explain: Bromine leaves as a brown vapour; molten lead collects at the cathode.

08-electrolysis-and-redox.q: "The magnesium ion is reduced" is preferred to "magnesium is reduced" because…
options: the species that exists before the electrons arrive is the ion, not the metal
08-electrolysis-and-redox.explain: Precision about the species is the mark: Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Mg. The metal is the RESULT of the reduction.

08-electrolysis-and-redox.q: Which ionic half-equation is balanced for both atoms AND charge?
08-electrolysis-and-redox.explain: Two chlorides (2−) → neutral Cl₂ + two electrons (2−): atoms 2=2, charge −2=−2. Check both counts, always.

08-electrolysis-and-redox.q: A reducing agent…
options: donates electrons (or removes oxygen) and is itself oxidised
08-electrolysis-and-redox.explain: It gives the electrons away — so it ends up oxidised. Carbon in metal extraction is the running example.

08-electrolysis-and-redox.q: Universal indicator near the ANODE of NaCl(aq) electrolysis would eventually show…
08-electrolysis-and-redox.explain: Chlorine forms there and bleaches the indicator — the cathode side is where it turns blue/purple (OH⁻).

08-electrolysis-and-redox.q: Which metal could NOT be extracted from its molten compound by electrolysis?
options: None — electrolysis works for all of them
08-electrolysis-and-redox.explain: Electrolysis works even for the most reactive metals — that is its point. (It's avoided where carbon is cheaper, not where it fails.)

08-electrolysis-and-redox.q: During electrolysis, electrons flow…
options: around the external circuit from anode to cathode
from cathode to anode inside the solution
08-electrolysis-and-redox.explain: Electrons take the wire; ions take the liquid. Two different charge carriers, one circuit.

08-electrolysis-and-redox.q: The reason copper(II) sulfate solution contains some OH⁻ ions is…
options: water dissociates slightly into H⁺ and OH⁻
08-electrolysis-and-redox.explain: From the water — 2023's Q5d, where "because the solution is alkaline" was the marked wrong answer (it isn't).

08-electrolysis-and-redox.q: In CuS + O₂ → Cu + SO₂, the sulfur is…
08-electrolysis-and-redox.explain: Sulfur picks up oxygen → SO₂: oxidation by the gain-of-oxygen definition (2021's extraction question).

08-electrolysis-and-redox.q: Why does electrolysis of ANY dilute sulfate or nitrate solution effectively electrolyse water?
options: Both the metal ion and the anion lose to H⁺ and OH⁻/water at the electrodes
08-electrolysis-and-redox.explain: Reactive metal stays in solution (H₂ forms); no halide means O₂ from water — so only H₂O is consumed and the salt remains.

08-electrolysis-and-redox.q: The negative electrode in electrolysis is called the…
08-electrolysis-and-redox.explain: Cathode = negative, attracts CATIONS (positive ions) which gain electrons. Anode = positive, attracts anions.

08-electrolysis-and-redox.q: Which substance would conduct electricity and be decomposed by it?
08-electrolysis-and-redox.explain: An electrolyte must have free-moving IONS: molten or dissolved ionic compounds. Copper conducts but is an element, so nothing decomposes; sugar solution has no ions.

08-electrolysis-and-redox.q: In the electrolysis of copper(II) sulfate solution, copper forms at the cathode because copper is…
08-electrolysis-and-redox.explain: The less reactive of the competing cations is discharged. Metals above hydrogen stay in solution and H₂ forms instead.

08-electrolysis-and-redox.q: Reduction can be defined as…
options: loss of electrons or gain of oxygen
gain of electrons or loss of oxygen
08-electrolysis-and-redox.explain: OIL RIG plus the oxygen version. Both definitions describe the same event from different angles.

08-electrolysis-and-redox.q: Which is a correctly written half-equation for reduction?
08-electrolysis-and-redox.explain: Electrons on the LEFT = being gained = reduction. The other three all show electrons being lost (oxidation).

08-electrolysis-and-redox.q: During the electrolysis of dilute sulfuric acid, the product at the negative electrode is…
08-electrolysis-and-redox.explain: H⁺ ions gain electrons: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂. Oxygen forms at the positive electrode from water.

08-electrolysis-and-redox.q: In the reaction Mg + CuSO₄ → MgSO₄ + Cu, magnesium is…
08-electrolysis-and-redox.explain: Mg → Mg²⁺ loses electrons (oxidation), so magnesium is the REDUCING agent; the copper ions are reduced.

08-electrolysis-and-redox.q: Electrolysis of molten aluminium oxide gives aluminium at the cathode and… at the anode.
08-electrolysis-and-redox.explain: The oxide ions are oxidised to O₂. (Industrially this oxygen burns the carbon anodes away, so they need regular replacement.)

08-electrolysis-and-redox.q: Which observation would you record at an electrode producing a gas?
08-electrolysis-and-redox.explain: Observations are what you SEE. Naming the gas is a conclusion drawn from a test, not an observation.

08-electrolysis-and-redox.q: Why must an ionic compound be molten or dissolved for electrolysis?
options: So that the ions are free to move to the electrodes
08-electrolysis-and-redox.explain: Mobile ions carry the charge through the electrolyte. In the solid lattice they are fixed, so no current flows.

09-metal-extraction.q: Which list is in order of decreasing reactivity?
09-metal-extraction.explain: K Na Li Ca Mg Al · Zn Fe · Cu Ag Au. Potassium tops the school's list; copper is near the bottom.

09-metal-extraction.q: Gold is found in the Earth's crust as the element because it is…
09-metal-extraction.explain: Too unreactive ever to have formed compounds — found native. Reactive metals are always locked up in ores.

09-metal-extraction.q: Aluminium cannot be extracted by heating its oxide with carbon because…
options: aluminium oxide has too high a melting point
aluminium is more reactive than carbon
09-metal-extraction.explain: Carbon can only strip oxygen from metals BELOW it in the series. Aluminium (above carbon) needs electrolysis of the molten compound. Same one-marker as 2023's magnesium question.

09-metal-extraction.q: Iron is extracted from its oxide using carbon because…
options: iron is more reactive than carbon
carbon is more reactive than iron and removes the oxygen
09-metal-extraction.explain: Carbon out-competes iron for the oxygen — it reduces the oxide. Cheapness is why carbon is preferred wherever it works.

09-metal-extraction.q: In 2CuO + C → 2Cu + CO₂, the role of carbon is…
options: reducing agent — it removes oxygen from the copper(II) oxide
09-metal-extraction.explain: The two-marker the school asked in both 2024 and 2025: reducing agent + removes oxygen from the named compound. "Reacts with the oxygen" was rejected.

09-metal-extraction.q: In the thermite reaction 2Al + Fe₂O₃ → Al₂O₃ + 2Fe, the species reduced is…
09-metal-extraction.explain: The OXIDE loses the oxygen. "Iron is reduced" was a named error in 2024 — iron is the product.

09-metal-extraction.q: Zinc powder is added to copper(II) sulfate solution. What happens?
options: The blue fades and copper coats the zinc
09-metal-extraction.explain: Zinc displaces copper: Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu. Blue Cu²⁺ leaves solution; pink-brown copper appears.

09-metal-extraction.q: Silver is placed in copper(II) sulfate solution. What happens?
09-metal-extraction.explain: A less reactive metal cannot displace a more reactive one. "No reaction" is itself the expected answer — say it confidently.

09-metal-extraction.q: An ore is…
options: any rock containing a metal compound worth extracting
a pure metal found in the ground
a metal oxide made in a furnace
09-metal-extraction.explain: Rock + enough metal compound to make extraction worthwhile. Native metals (gold) are the exception — no compound, no ore chemistry needed.

09-metal-extraction.q: Metals above carbon in the reactivity series are extracted by…
09-metal-extraction.explain: Carbon can't reduce their oxides, so electrons are supplied directly at the cathode — expensive, but reactivity forces it (aluminium is the spec's example).

09-metal-extraction.q: In stage 1 of copper extraction, sulfur in the ore is described as oxidised because it…
09-metal-extraction.explain: Apply the definition: gained oxygen. "It forms SO₂" merely names the product — the 2021 scheme wanted the definition-level reason.

09-metal-extraction.q: The cheap reducing agent used industrially to extract iron is…
09-metal-extraction.explain: Coke is cheap carbon. Aluminium works chemically (thermite!) but costs far more than the iron it would win — economics picks carbon everywhere it can work.

09-metal-extraction.q: The reactivity series orders metals by…
options: how vigorously they react / how strongly they hold their compounds
09-metal-extraction.explain: It ranks reactivity — which then predicts displacement, extraction method and acid behaviour.

09-metal-extraction.q: Which metal is MOST reactive?
09-metal-extraction.explain: K tops the school list: K Na Li Ca Mg Al · Zn Fe · Cu Ag Au.

09-metal-extraction.q: Which metal is LEAST reactive?
09-metal-extraction.explain: Gold sits at the bottom — so unreactive it is found native.

09-metal-extraction.q: A metal that displaces copper from copper sulfate solution but not magnesium from magnesium sulfate lies…
09-metal-extraction.explain: Displaces what is below it, loses to what is above — the sandwich logic used to place unknown metals.

09-metal-extraction.q: Iron + copper(II) sulfate → iron(II) sulfate + copper is an example of…
09-metal-extraction.explain: More reactive iron takes the sulfate from less reactive copper.

09-metal-extraction.q: Carbon can extract a metal from its oxide only if the metal is…
09-metal-extraction.explain: Carbon must out-compete the metal for oxygen — possible only for Zn, Fe, Cu and below.

09-metal-extraction.q: The extraction of iron from iron(III) oxide using carbon is an example of the oxide being…
09-metal-extraction.explain: The oxide LOSES its oxygen — reduction. Carbon (the reducing agent) is oxidised to CO₂.

09-metal-extraction.q: Aluminium is extracted by electrolysis rather than carbon because…
options: aluminium is more reactive than carbon
09-metal-extraction.explain: Carbon cannot strip oxygen from a metal above it. The expense is forced by the chemistry, not chosen.

09-metal-extraction.q: Gold is found 'native'. This means…
09-metal-extraction.explain: Too unreactive to form compounds — it sits in the crust as the metal itself.

09-metal-extraction.q: In the thermite reaction, the magnesium fuse is needed because…
options: the reaction needs a large initial energy input to start
09-metal-extraction.explain: Thermite has a high activation energy — the burning fuse supplies it; after that the reaction's own heat sustains it.

09-metal-extraction.q: Which pairing of metal and extraction method is correct?
options: Iron — heat the oxide with carbon
09-metal-extraction.explain: Fe is below carbon → carbon reduction. Na needs electrolysis; Zn can use carbon; gold needs nothing.

09-metal-extraction.q: An ore is worth mining when…
options: it contains any metal at all
it contains enough metal (compound) to make extraction economic
it is close to the surface
09-metal-extraction.explain: "Enough to be worth extracting" is part of the definition — economics is built into the word ore.

09-metal-extraction.q: Zinc + iron(II) sulfate solution →…
09-metal-extraction.explain: Zinc is above iron, so it displaces it. (Iron + zinc sulfate would be the no-reaction direction.)

09-metal-extraction.q: Which observation shows displacement is happening in copper(II) sulfate + zinc?
options: The blue fades and a brown solid appears
09-metal-extraction.explain: Blue Cu²⁺ leaves the solution as brown copper metal appears on the zinc.

09-metal-extraction.q: The role of carbon in 2Fe₂O₃ + 3C → 4Fe + 3CO₂ is…
09-metal-extraction.explain: It removes the oxygen from the iron(III) oxide — same two-marker as the copper and calcium phosphide versions.

09-metal-extraction.q: Which metal is found in the crust ONLY in compounds?
09-metal-extraction.explain: Reactive metals are always combined; only the unreactive tail of the series occurs native.

09-metal-extraction.q: Why is extraction by carbon preferred wherever possible?
options: Carbon is a stronger reducing agent than electricity
Coke is much cheaper than electricity
09-metal-extraction.explain: Economics: heating with cheap coke beats paying for continuous current — which is reserved for metals above carbon.

09-metal-extraction.q: "Comment on this extraction process" questions (spec 2.24C) should be anchored to…
options: the metal's position relative to carbon, and what reduces what
09-metal-extraction.explain: Position → method; then name the reduction and the reducing agent. Detailed process knowledge is explicitly not required.

09-metal-extraction.q: Copper displaces silver from silver nitrate solution. What does this show?
options: Silver is more reactive than copper
Copper is more reactive than silver
09-metal-extraction.explain: The displacer is always the more reactive metal — this experiment places Cu above Ag in the series.

09-metal-extraction.q: Which statement about the thermite redox is fully correct?
options: Iron is reduced and aluminium oxidised
Iron(III) oxide is reduced and aluminium is oxidised
Aluminium is reduced and iron oxidised
09-metal-extraction.explain: Name the compound: the OXIDE loses oxygen (reduced); aluminium gains it (oxidised). "Iron is reduced" lost the mark in 2024.

09-metal-extraction.q: The reactivity series position of hydrogen matters because…
options: metals below hydrogen do not react with dilute acids
hydrogen is the strongest reducing agent
09-metal-extraction.explain: Cu, Ag, Au sit below H: no reaction with dilute acid, and their ions win at the cathode — the same fact doing double duty in electrolysis.

09-metal-extraction.q: Which metal is extracted by heating its oxide with carbon?
09-metal-extraction.explain: Iron sits below carbon in the reactivity series, so carbon can take its oxygen. The other three are above carbon and need electrolysis.

09-metal-extraction.q: A metal above carbon in the reactivity series must be extracted by…
09-metal-extraction.explain: Carbon cannot reduce it, so electrons are supplied directly at the cathode — expensive, but the chemistry gives no choice.

09-metal-extraction.q: Which metal would displace zinc from zinc sulfate solution?
09-metal-extraction.explain: Only a metal ABOVE zinc can displace it — magnesium. Copper, silver and gold are all below zinc.

09-metal-extraction.q: In 2CuO + C → 2Cu + CO₂, which substance is oxidised?
09-metal-extraction.explain: Carbon gains oxygen → CO₂ (oxidised), which is why it is the reducing agent; the copper oxide loses oxygen (reduced).

09-metal-extraction.q: Why is gold found as the uncombined metal?
09-metal-extraction.explain: Unreactive metals never formed compounds — they occur native. That is also why gold needs no extraction chemistry.

09-metal-extraction.q: A metal displaces copper but not magnesium from their salt solutions. It lies…
09-metal-extraction.explain: It beats copper but loses to magnesium — the sandwich test for placing an unknown metal in the series.

09-metal-extraction.q: The main reason carbon reduction is preferred to electrolysis where possible is…
options: coke is far cheaper than electricity
09-metal-extraction.explain: Pure economics. Electrolysis is reserved for the metals whose reactivity forces it.

09-metal-extraction.q: In the thermite reaction, aluminium acts as the…
09-metal-extraction.explain: It removes the oxygen from iron(III) oxide, being oxidised itself — the same role carbon plays in a blast furnace.

09-metal-extraction.q: What would you observe when magnesium ribbon is placed in copper(II) sulfate solution?
options: The blue fades and a brown solid forms on the ribbon
A gas is given off and the solution turns blue
09-metal-extraction.explain: Displacement: Cu²⁺ leaves solution (blue fades) and copper deposits on the magnesium.

09-metal-extraction.q: Which statement about ores is correct?
options: An ore is a pure metal
An ore is a rock containing enough metal compound to be worth extracting
09-metal-extraction.explain: The 'worth extracting' part is in the definition — economics decides whether a rock counts as an ore.

10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.q: A hydrocarbon is a compound containing…
10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.explain: The word ONLY is the mark. CO₂ and glucose contain carbon but are not hydrocarbons.

10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.q: Crude oil is…
10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.explain: A mixture — which is why it can be separated physically (by distillation) without any chemical change.

10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.q: In the fractionating column, each vapour condenses when…
options: the column temperature falls below its boiling point
10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.explain: The condensation-at-the-boiling-point link is the M4 of the three-years-running four-marker. "Turns to liquid" without the reason does not score.

10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.q: The temperature in a fractionating column is…
10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.explain: Hot at the bottom where the vaporised crude enters, cooler toward the top — the gradient that sorts the fractions.

10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.q: The fraction with the LOWEST boiling point is…
10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.explain: Shortest molecules, weakest intermolecular forces, lowest bp — they exit at the top (many never condense at all). Bitumen is the opposite extreme.

10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.q: The fuel oil fraction is used for…
10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.explain: Gasoline → cars; kerosene → jets; diesel → lorries; fuel oil → ships/power stations; bitumen → roads. 2022 and 2024 both asked fuel oil.

10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.q: Going down the column, the fractions become…
10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.explain: Longer chains at the bottom: higher boiling point, darker colour, higher viscosity, LESS flammable.

10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.q: A long-chain alkane boils higher than a short one because…
options: the intermolecular forces between its molecules are stronger
the forces between its atoms are stronger
10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.explain: Forces BETWEEN MOLECULES — 2024's scheme rejected "between atoms" and gave nothing for broken covalent bonds.

10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.q: The general formula of the alkanes is…
10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.explain: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ — methane CH₄, ethane C₂H₆, propane C₃H₈… (CₙH₂ₙ is the alkenes.)

10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.q: The name of the alkane C₃H₈ is…
10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.explain: Three carbons = prop-, saturated = -ane. Spelling counts: 2023's marker rejected "triane".

10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.q: Isomers are compounds with…
options: the same chemical formula and structure
the same molecular formula but different structural formulae
different molecular formulae but the same shape
10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.explain: SAME molecular formula, DIFFERENT structure. "Chemical formula" lost the mark in 2023 — the precise term matters.

10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.q: The two isomers of C₄H₁₀ are…
10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.explain: Straight-chain butane and branched methylpropane. Butene has a double bond (different formula); pentane is C₅H₁₂.

10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.q: In a displayed formula you must show…
options: every atom and every bond, including all C–H bonds
10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.explain: Displayed = every bond drawn. A –CH₃ written as a lump was rejected in 2021's mark scheme.

10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.q: Complete combustion of an alkane produces…
10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.explain: CO₂ + H₂O. "Lots of students said hydrogen instead of water" — 2025's commentary. CO belongs to INCOMPLETE combustion.

10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.q: Carbon monoxide forms when a fuel burns in…
10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.explain: Limited oxygen → incomplete combustion → CO (and soot). Plenty of air gives CO₂.

10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.q: Carbon monoxide is poisonous because it…
options: reduces the capacity of the blood to transport oxygen
10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.explain: The spec's own wording. If you mention haemoglobin you must still mention oxygen — 2025's scheme checked.

10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.q: Sulfur dioxide in the atmosphere comes from…
options: nitrogen in the air reacting in engines
sulfur impurities in the fuel burning
10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.explain: The fuel CONTAINS sulfur; burning gives SO₂ → acid rain. The nitrogen chain is separate: N₂ + O₂ from the AIR react at engine temperatures → NOₓ.

10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.q: CH₄ + Br₂ → CH₃Br + HBr is classified as…
10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.explain: A bromine atom substitutes for a hydrogen — needs UV light. "Displacement" and "reduction" were 2025's popular wrong answers; addition needs a C=C double bond.

10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.q: The condition required for methane to react with bromine is…
10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.explain: UV (sunlight accepted). The schemes ignore heat — light is the answer.

10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.q: Catalytic cracking converts long alkanes into…
10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.explain: Silica/alumina catalyst at 600–700 °C: shorter alkanes (fuel) + alkenes (plastics feedstock) — done because demand for short fractions outstrips supply.

10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.q: The compounds in crude oil are separated by fractional distillation because they have…
10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.explain: The whole column works on boiling-point differences — that is what a fraction shares.

10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.q: Where does the crude oil enter the fractionating column?
options: Near the bottom, as hot vapour
It is poured over the outside
10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.explain: Heated and vaporised first, entering low where the column is hottest.

10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.q: The fraction used as aircraft fuel is…
10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.explain: Kerosene (paraffin) = jet fuel. Gasoline cars, diesel lorries, fuel oil ships, bitumen roads.

10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.q: Bitumen leaves the column at the bottom because it has…
10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.explain: Longest chains → strongest IMF → boils (and condenses) hottest → never rises.

10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.q: The general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ tells you that hexane (6 carbons) is…
10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.explain: 2 × 6 + 2 = 14 hydrogens: C₆H₁₄.

10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.q: Alkanes are described as saturated because…
options: they contain only single carbon–carbon bonds
10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.explain: Every carbon already holds four single bonds — no capacity to add more atoms (hence substitution, not addition).

10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.q: Members of a homologous series differ from their neighbours by…
10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.explain: Each step adds CH₂ — the reason the general formula works and boiling points climb steadily.

10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.q: The molecular formula of the alkane with structural formula CH₃CH₂CH₃ is…
10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.explain: Count: 3 carbons, 3+2+3 = 8 hydrogens — propane.

10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.q: The empirical formula of ethane (C₂H₆) is…
10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.explain: Divide by the common factor 2: CH₃. Molecular and empirical formulae differ whenever the ratio simplifies.

10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.q: How many isomers does C₅H₁₂ have?
10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.explain: Pentane, 2-methylbutane, 2,2-dimethylpropane — the paper gives one and asks you to draw the other two.

10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.q: Which is NOT an isomer consideration when drawing C₄H₁₀ structures?
10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.explain: Isomers keep the SAME molecular formula — changing the carbon count makes a different compound entirely.

10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.q: A molecule drawn bent versus straight but with identical connections is…
10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.explain: Rotating or bending bonds doesn't change what is bonded to what — a classic false 'isomer' pair that scores nothing.

10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.q: Complete combustion of methane is…
10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.explain: CO₂ and WATER, balanced with 2O₂. CO and soot belong to incomplete combustion; H₂ is never a combustion product.

10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.q: The yellow, sooty flame of a Bunsen with the air hole closed indicates…
10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.explain: Limited air → carbon particles glowing yellow and CO forming — the visible signature of incomplete burning.

10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.q: Carbon monoxide is dangerous partly because it is…
10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.explain: No colour, no smell, no warning — while it quietly reduces the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity.

10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.q: Oxides of nitrogen form in car engines because…
options: engine temperatures are high enough for nitrogen and oxygen from the AIR to react
nitrogen burns in the fuel tank
10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.explain: The nitrogen comes from the air, not the fuel — the distinction that carries the mark.

10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.q: Acid rain is caused by…
options: sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen
10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.explain: SO₂ (fuel impurities) and NOₓ (engine heat). CO₂/greenhouse belongs to a different question — mixing them cost marks in 2025.

10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.q: One effect of acid rain accepted by the schemes is…
10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.explain: The two standard consequences: aquatic life killed, carbonate stone eroded.

10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.q: In CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl (in UV light), the organic product is…
10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.explain: One H swapped for Cl: chloromethane, CH₃Cl. HCl is the inorganic co-product; mono-substitution only at this level.

10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.q: Why does the methane–bromine reaction not happen in the dark?
options: UV light is needed to provide the energy to start the reaction
10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.explain: The UV splits the Br₂ to kick things off — no light, no reaction, however long you wait.

10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.q: Alkenes differ from alkanes in having…
10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.explain: Alkenes (CₙH₂ₙ) are unsaturated: one C=C. They appear here as the second product of cracking.

10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.q: The conditions for catalytic cracking are…
options: high pressure and an iron catalyst
10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.explain: Spec 4.17 verbatim: silica/alumina, 600–700 °C.

10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.q: Cracking C₁₂H₂₆ could give C₈H₁₈ plus…
10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.explain: Atoms must balance: 12−8 = 4 carbons, 26−18 = 8 hydrogens → C₄H₈, an alkene (as cracking must produce).

10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.q: Cracking is economically necessary because…
options: demand for short fractions exceeds their supply in crude oil
the column cannot separate long chains
10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.explain: Petrol demand outstrips what distillation yields; surplus heavy fractions are cracked down to match supply to demand.

10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.q: A fuel is defined as a substance that…
10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.explain: Spec 4.11's definition — heat energy on burning. Not all fuels are hydrocarbons and not all hydrocarbons are used as fuels.

10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.q: Crude oil is separated by fractional distillation because the hydrocarbons have different…
10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.explain: Boiling point is what the column sorts on — which follows from chain length and intermolecular forces.

10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.q: Which fraction has the shortest hydrocarbon molecules?
10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.explain: Shortest chains, weakest forces, lowest boiling point — they leave at the top. Bitumen is the opposite extreme.

10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.q: The molecular formula of the alkane with 4 carbon atoms is…
10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.explain: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ with n = 4: 2(4) + 2 = 10 → C₄H₁₀, butane. C₄H₈ would be an alkene.

10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.q: Complete combustion of a hydrocarbon requires…
10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.explain: Plenty of oxygen gives CO₂ + H₂O. Limited oxygen gives carbon monoxide and soot.

10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.q: Which gas produced by burning fuels causes acid rain?
10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.explain: SO₂ (from sulfur impurities) and oxides of nitrogen (from engine heat). CO₂ is the greenhouse gas — a different problem.

10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.q: Isomers must have the same…
10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.explain: Same molecular formula, different structures — and therefore usually different physical properties like boiling point.

10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.q: The reaction between an alkane and a halogen requires…
10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.explain: UV light starts it. The reaction type is substitution — one hydrogen swapped for a halogen atom.

10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.q: Cracking produces…
10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.explain: Long chains break into a shorter alkane plus an alkene — matching supply to the high demand for short fractions.

10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.q: Carbon monoxide is dangerous because it…
options: reduces the capacity of the blood to carry oxygen
10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.explain: The spec's wording — and it is colourless and odourless, so there is no warning.

10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.q: Which property increases going DOWN the fractionating column?
10-crude-oil-and-alkanes.explain: Down = longer chains = higher boiling point, darker colour, more viscous — and LESS flammable/volatile.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: Why do lithium, sodium and potassium have similar chemical reactions?
options: They all have one electron in their outer shell
They all have the same number of shells
They all have the same number of protons
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Reactions happen at the outer shell. All Group 1 atoms have one outer electron, so they react in the same way.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: What are the products when sodium reacts with water?
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂. A Group 1 metal and water always give a metal hydroxide and hydrogen.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: Phenolphthalein is added to the solution left after sodium reacts with water. What colour does it turn?
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Phenolphthalein turns pink in alkali, and the solution contains OH⁻ ions. The 2024 mark scheme rejected red and purple.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: Which observation is seen when potassium reacts with water but NOT when lithium does?
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Potassium releases so much heat that the hydrogen ignites with a lilac flame. Lithium reacts too slowly for that.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: What is the final colour of universal indicator after sodium has reacted with the water it is in?
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: The sodium hydroxide solution is alkaline, so universal indicator turns blue or purple.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: Why does sodium melt into a ball when it reacts with water?
options: It reacts with oxygen dissolved in the water
The reaction is exothermic and sodium has a low melting point
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: The heat given out is enough to melt sodium, which melts at 98 °C.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: Which is the correct order of reactivity, most reactive first?
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Reactivity increases down Group 1, so potassium is the most reactive of the three.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: Why is potassium more reactive than sodium?
options: Potassium has more protons, so it attracts electrons more strongly
Potassium has more outer electrons to lose
Potassium's outer electron is further from the nucleus, so it is less strongly attracted
Potassium has a smaller atomic radius
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Potassium has more shells, so its outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded. It is lost more easily.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: Why are Group 1 metals stored under oil?
options: To stop them reacting with air and water
To make them easier to cut
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: The oil keeps oxygen and water away from the metal, so it does not tarnish or react.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: A freshly cut piece of lithium is shiny but slowly goes dull. What causes this?
options: It reacts with oxygen to form an oxide
It reacts with nitrogen to form a nitride
It melts in the warm air
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: The shiny metal reacts with oxygen in the air to form a dull oxide layer. This is called tarnishing.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: The melting points of Li, Na and K are 181 °C, 98 °C and 63 °C. Which is the best prediction for rubidium's melting point?
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Melting point decreases down Group 1, so rubidium's must be below 63 °C. Its actual melting point is 39 °C.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: What is the formula of rubidium hydroxide?
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Rubidium is in Group 1, so it forms Rb⁺ ions. One Rb⁺ balances one OH⁻.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: Which equation for lithium reacting with water is correctly balanced?
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: There are two H atoms in H₂, so two LiOH and two H₂O are needed, and therefore two Li.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: 0.46 g of sodium reacts with water. How many moles of hydrogen are made? [Aᵣ of Na = 23]
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: 0.46 ÷ 23 = 0.020 mol of Na. Two Na give one H₂, so 0.010 mol of H₂ is made.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: What colour and state is chlorine at room temperature?
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Chlorine is a pale yellow-green gas. Bromine is the red-brown liquid and iodine is the grey-black solid.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: What colour and state is bromine at room temperature?
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Bromine is a red-brown liquid that gives off an orange-brown vapour.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: What colour is iodine vapour?
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Solid iodine is grey-black, but when it is warmed it gives a purple vapour.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: Which halogen has the palest colour?
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Colour darkens down Group 7, so fluorine, at the top, is the palest (pale yellow).

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: Which halogen is a solid at room temperature?
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Melting points rise down Group 7. Iodine and astatine are solids, bromine is a liquid, and chlorine and fluorine are gases.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: Why do the boiling points of the halogens increase down the group?
options: The intermolecular forces get stronger as the molecules get bigger
The atoms lose electrons more easily
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Boiling overcomes the forces between molecules. These get stronger as the molecules get larger. No covalent bonds are broken.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: Chlorine water is added to potassium bromide solution. What is seen?
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Chlorine is more reactive, so it displaces bromine, and bromine in solution is orange.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: Bromine water is added to potassium chloride solution. What happens?
options: There is no change — it stays orange
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Bromine is less reactive than chlorine, so it cannot displace chlorine. The mixture stays orange.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: Bromine water is added to potassium iodide solution. What colour does the solution become?
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Bromine displaces iodine, and iodine in solution is brown.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: Which mixture will NOT react?
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Iodine is less reactive than bromine, so it cannot displace bromine from potassium bromide.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: Which is the correct ionic equation for chlorine reacting with bromide ions?
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Two Br⁻ ions make one Br₂ molecule, and Cl₂ becomes two Cl⁻ ions. Atoms and charges both balance.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: In the reaction Cl₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + I₂, which species is oxidised?
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Iodide ions lose electrons to form iodine (2I⁻ → I₂ + 2e⁻). Loss of electrons is oxidation.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: In a halogen displacement reaction, what is the role of the more reactive halogen?
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: The halogen takes electrons from the halide ion. It is reduced and acts as the oxidising agent.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: In the reaction between chlorine and potassium bromide solution, which ions are spectator ions?
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: K⁺ ions are unchanged in the reaction, so they are left out of the ionic equation.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: Which is the correct half-equation for chlorine in a displacement reaction?
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Each chlorine atom gains one electron, so Cl₂ gains two electrons to form 2Cl⁻. This is reduction.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: Why is fluorine more reactive than chlorine?
options: Fluorine's outer shell is closer to the nucleus, so it attracts an extra electron more strongly
Fluorine has more electrons in its outer shell
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Fluorine (2.7) has fewer shells than chlorine (2.8.7), so the nucleus pulls an incoming electron more strongly.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: Going down Group 7, what happens to the reactivity of the halogens?
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: The outer shell gets further from the nucleus, so an extra electron is gained less readily.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: What is the best prediction for what happens when chlorine water is added to sodium astatide solution?
options: No reaction, because astatine is more reactive
Astatine is displaced, because chlorine is more reactive
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Astatine is at the bottom of Group 7, so it is the least reactive halogen. Chlorine displaces it.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: What is the correct equation for lithium reacting with chlorine?
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Chlorine is diatomic (Cl₂) and lithium chloride is LiCl, so two lithium atoms are needed.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: Why is neon unreactive?
options: It has a full outer shell, so it does not need to lose, gain or share electrons
It is a gas at room temperature
It has one electron in its outer shell
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Neon is 2.8, with a full outer shell. That is stable, so it does not form bonds.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: Helium has only 2 outer electrons. Why is it still unreactive?
options: 2 electrons fill its only shell, so its outer shell is full
It is too light to react
Its electrons are too far from the nucleus
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Helium's first shell holds a maximum of 2 electrons, so helium has a full outer shell like the other noble gases.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: Magnesium is used to extract titanium from TiCl₄ in a container of argon. Why argon rather than air?
options: Argon is unreactive, whereas oxygen in air would oxidise the magnesium
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Argon does not react with the hot metal. In air, oxygen would react with the magnesium and titanium.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: Which is the least reactive gas in the atmosphere?
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Argon is a noble gas with a full outer shell, so it is the least reactive gas in air.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: Noble gases exist as single atoms. What is the word for this?
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Noble gas atoms do not bond to each other, so they exist as separate atoms. They are monatomic.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: Why are filament light bulbs filled with argon?
options: The hot filament does not react with argon
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Argon is unreactive. In air, the hot filament would react with oxygen and burn out.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: Which statement about Group 1 and Group 7 is correct?
options: Both groups get more reactive down the group
Group 1 atoms gain electrons; Group 7 atoms lose electrons
Both groups get less reactive down the group
Group 1 gets more reactive down the group; Group 7 gets less reactive
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: The outer shell gets further from the nucleus in both groups. That makes losing an electron easier (Group 1) but gaining one harder (Group 7).

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: What is the approximate percentage by volume of nitrogen in dry air?
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Dry air is about 78% nitrogen, which is roughly four-fifths. In 2024 the multiple-choice answer was given as 80%.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: What is the approximate percentage by volume of oxygen in dry air?
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Oxygen is about 21%, roughly one-fifth of dry air. 0.9% is argon and 78% is nitrogen.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: Which gas makes up about 1% of dry air?
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Argon is about 0.9%, the trace gas with the highest percentage. Carbon dioxide is only about 0.04%.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: Which of these gases has the lowest percentage by volume in dry air?
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Carbon dioxide is about 0.04%, much less than argon (0.9%), oxygen (21%) or nitrogen (78%).

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: Which gas is NOT normally found in the atmosphere?
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Hydrogen is not normally found in the atmosphere (2022 Edexcel 2C Q1). The other three are all present.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: Why is the composition of air usually given for DRY air?
options: Water vapour is a greenhouse gas
The amount of water vapour varies from place to place and day to day
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Water vapour changes a lot, so it is left out. That way the percentages of the other gases stay fixed.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: Why does argon not react with hot copper or iron?
options: It has a full outer shell of electrons
It is a gas at room temperature
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Argon has a full outer shell, so it does not gain, lose or share electrons. Being a gas has nothing to do with it.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: In the iron wool and test tube experiment, why does water rise up the tube?
options: The iron dissolves in the water
The water evaporates into the tube
The iron uses up the oxygen, so the gas volume decreases
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Iron reacts with oxygen to form solid rust. The gas volume falls and water moves up to fill the space.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: Why must the iron wool be wet in the rusting experiment?
options: Water is needed for iron to rust
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Iron needs both oxygen and water to rust, so the iron must be wet for the oxygen to be used up.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: Why is iron powder better than an iron nail for finding the % of oxygen in air?
options: Powder has a larger surface area, so it reacts faster
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: A larger surface area means more collisions per second, so the oxygen is used up sooner. The final result is the same.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: What colour is rust?
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Rust is brown (orange-brown or red-brown was also allowed). The 2022 scheme ignored 'red' on its own.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: What is the formula of the iron oxide in rust?
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Rust is hydrated iron(III) oxide. Fe³⁺ and O²⁻ give Fe₂O₃.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: A gas column in an inverted tube falls from 75 mm to 30 mm as the oxygen is used. What is the percentage of oxygen?
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: The decrease is 45 mm, and 45 ÷ 75 × 100 = 60%. 40% is the gas left, which scored only 1 of 2 in 2023.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: A flask and tube hold 260 cm³. The syringe falls from 90 cm³ to 22 cm³. What is the % oxygen?
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Oxygen = 68 cm³ and total air = 260 + 90 = 350 cm³, so 68 ÷ 350 × 100 = 19.4%. 26.2% leaves out the syringe air.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: In the gas-syringe method, what is the total starting volume of air?
options: The flask volume plus the starting syringe reading
The flask volume minus the final syringe reading
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: The flask and syringe are connected, so the iron removes oxygen from both. The total is the apparatus plus the starting syringe reading.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: How do you know all the oxygen has reacted in the heated-copper method?
options: The syringe readings stay the same
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: When repeated passes give the same reading, no more oxygen is being removed.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: Why is the copper heated in the two-syringe experiment?
options: To increase the rate so the copper reacts with the oxygen
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Cold copper reacts with oxygen far too slowly. Heating gives the particles enough energy to react quickly.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: What is the black solid formed when copper reacts with oxygen?
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: 2Cu + O₂ → 2CuO, which is black copper(II) oxide. The mark scheme rejected copper(I) oxide.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: Why should the apparatus cool to room temperature before the final syringe reading?
options: Warm gas takes up a larger volume
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Gas expands when hot. A warm final reading is too big, which makes the % oxygen too low.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: Syringe A reads 78 cm³ at the start and 58 cm³ at the end. The tube holds 175 cm³. What is the % oxygen in the mixture?
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Oxygen = 20 cm³ and total = 175 + 78 = 253 cm³, so 20 ÷ 253 × 100 = 7.9% (2022 Jan Edexcel 1C Q4).

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: Which non-metal is named in the spec for finding the % of oxygen in air?
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: The spec names iron (a metal) and phosphorus (a non-metal) for this experiment.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: Which observation is seen when magnesium burns in oxygen?
options: A blue flame and a choking gas
A bright white light and a white powder
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Magnesium burns with a bright white light and leaves white magnesium oxide powder. 'White precipitate' was rejected.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: Which is the correct balanced equation for magnesium burning?
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Oxygen is O₂ and magnesium oxide is MgO, so you need 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: What are the state symbols in 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO?
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Magnesium is a solid, oxygen a gas and magnesium oxide a solid: (s), (g), (s), as in the school's 2025 Q4(b).

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: What is seen when sulfur burns in oxygen?
options: A blue flame and a colourless, choking gas
An orange flame and black smoke
No flame, just a brown solid
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Sulfur burns with a blue flame to form sulfur dioxide, a colourless gas with a choking smell.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: What is the product when hydrogen burns in oxygen?
options: Hydrogen oxide gas that is acidic
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. The only product is water.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: What type of oxide does a metal form?
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Metal oxides are basic. Those that dissolve give alkaline solutions with a pH above 7.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: Sulfur dioxide dissolves in water. What would the solution do to blue litmus?
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: SO₂ is an acidic oxide, so its solution contains H⁺ ions and turns blue litmus red.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: Which ion makes a solution of sulfur dioxide acidic?
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Acidic solutions contain hydrogen ions, H⁺ (school 2021 Q10(c)).

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: An element conducts electricity and its oxide gives a solution of pH 11. The element is most likely:
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Conducting electricity and forming a basic oxide are both properties of metals.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: Which element forms a basic oxide?
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Lithium is a metal, so its oxide is basic. This was the 2024 Edexcel 1C Q1(a) answer. The others are non-metals.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: Where are non-metals found in the Periodic Table?
options: On the right, beyond the stepped line
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Non-metals are on the right of the stepped line (plus hydrogen). Metals are on the left and in the centre.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: Which non-metal element conducts electricity?
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Graphite has delocalised electrons, so it conducts. It is the usual exception to 'non-metals do not conduct'.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: What type of reaction happens when copper(II) carbonate is heated?
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Heat breaks one substance into two: CuCO₃ → CuO + CO₂. This is thermal decomposition.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: What colour change is seen when copper(II) carbonate is heated?
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Copper(II) carbonate is green, and copper(II) oxide is black. Both 2022 and 2023 asked this.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: Which equation shows the thermal decomposition of copper(II) carbonate?
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: A metal carbonate decomposes to the metal oxide and carbon dioxide: CuCO₃ → CuO + CO₂.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: 7.40 g of XCO₃ gives off 2.20 g of CO₂ when heated. What is the Mᵣ of XCO₃?
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: n(CO₂) = 2.20 ÷ 44 = 0.05 mol = n(XCO₃), so Mᵣ = 7.40 ÷ 0.05 = 148. Then Aᵣ(X) = 88, which is strontium.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: Which of these reactions produces carbon dioxide?
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Complete combustion of a hydrocarbon gives carbon dioxide and water. Mg + HCl gives hydrogen.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: Why is an increasing amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere a problem?
options: It is a greenhouse gas that may contribute to climate change
It is the main cause of acid rain
It reduces the amount of nitrogen
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: CO₂ traps heat in the atmosphere. Mark schemes reject answers about the ozone layer and ignore acid rain.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: Which is an accepted effect of increasing carbon dioxide levels?
options: More ozone in the upper atmosphere
Rising sea levels from melting ice caps
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Climate change leads to melting ice caps, rising sea levels, flooding and wildfires. Oceans becoming more acidic is also accepted.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: Which two substances must both be present for iron to rust?
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: Iron rusts only when both oxygen (air) and water are present. Salt speeds rusting up but is not needed.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: What is the chemical name for rust?
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: Rust is hydrated iron(III) oxide, simplified formula Fe₂O₃. Iron(II) oxide is rejected by the mark schemes.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: What type of reaction is the rusting of iron?
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: Iron gains oxygen (and loses electrons) when it rusts, so rusting is oxidation.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: Which metal is used to galvanise iron?
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: Galvanising means coating iron or steel with a layer of zinc.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: A galvanised bucket is scratched through to the steel, but the steel does not rust. Why?
options: Zinc is more reactive than iron, so the zinc is oxidised instead of the iron
Zinc is less reactive than iron, so it seals the scratch
The zinc rusts instead of the iron
The scratch fills with zinc oxide paint
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: Zinc is more reactive, so it corrodes (is oxidised) instead of the iron. Saying zinc 'rusts' is rejected — only iron rusts.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: Which of these is a barrier method of rust prevention?
options: Connecting to a less reactive metal
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: Greasing coats the iron so water and oxygen cannot reach it. Magnesium blocks are sacrificial protection, not a barrier.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: Why are blocks of magnesium attached to the steel hull of a ship?
options: Magnesium is less reactive than iron, so it protects it
Magnesium is more reactive than iron, so it corrodes instead of the iron
Magnesium reacts with salt to make a waterproof layer
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: This is sacrificial protection: the more reactive magnesium is oxidised instead of the iron.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: In the rusting experiment, why is a layer of oil put on top of the boiled water?
options: To stop air dissolving back into the water
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: Boiling removes dissolved air; the oil layer stops oxygen dissolving back in, so the tube has water but no oxygen.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: What is the job of anhydrous calcium chloride in a rusting experiment?
options: It absorbs water vapour, keeping the air dry
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: Anhydrous calcium chloride is a drying agent; that tube shows iron does not rust without water.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: Which tube will show rust after a week?
options: Nail in boiled water under a layer of oil
Nail in tap water, open to the air
Nail in dry air with calcium chloride, stoppered
Nail in a sealed tube of dry nitrogen
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: Only the tube with both water and oxygen rusts.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: Why does iron powder rust faster than an iron nail?
options: Powder is more reactive than iron in a nail
Powder has a larger surface area
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: A larger surface area gives a faster reaction — the same metal, just more of it exposed.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: What is observed when magnesium ribbon is added to dilute hydrochloric acid?
options: Vigorous fizzing and the tube gets warm
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: Magnesium is high in the series, so it reacts fast with acid to give hydrogen; the reaction is exothermic.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: Which metal does NOT react with dilute sulfuric acid?
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: Copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series, so it cannot displace hydrogen from acids.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: What are the products when zinc reacts with dilute sulfuric acid?
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: Metal + acid → salt + hydrogen: Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: Which is the correct equation for iron reacting with dilute sulfuric acid?
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: Iron forms iron(II) sulfate and hydrogen with dilute sulfuric acid; the equation is balanced 1:1:1:1.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: Give the word equation for aluminium reacting with hydrochloric acid.
options: aluminium + hydrochloric acid → aluminium chlorine + hydrogen
aluminium + hydrochloric acid → aluminium oxide + hydrogen
aluminium + hydrochloric acid → aluminium chloride + water
aluminium + hydrochloric acid → aluminium chloride + hydrogen
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: Hydrochloric acid makes chlorides, and a metal with acid gives hydrogen.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: Why is the reaction of sodium with dilute hydrochloric acid not done in school?
options: Sodium does not react with acid
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: Sodium is very high in the series; its reaction with acid is violent. 'Vigorous' or 'volatile' alone scored nothing in 2024.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: Metal A reacts very fast with water. Metal B does not react with water but fizzes slowly in acid. Metal C does not react with either. Which could B be?
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: B is above hydrogen but does not react with cold water — zinc or iron fits. Potassium and sodium react fast with water; gold does not react with acid.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: What forms when magnesium reacts with steam?
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: With steam the product is the oxide: Mg + H₂O → MgO + H₂.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: Which is the balanced equation for calcium reacting with water?
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: Metal + water → metal hydroxide + hydrogen; two water molecules balance the OH groups.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: Iron is added to copper(II) sulfate solution. What is the solid that forms?
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: Iron displaces copper, which forms as a pink-brown solid. The blue colour fades to pale green.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: Why is there no reaction when iron is added to magnesium sulfate solution?
options: Iron is less reactive than magnesium
Iron is more reactive than magnesium
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: A less reactive metal cannot displace a more reactive one from its compound.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: Magnesium is added to magnesium sulfate solution. Why is there no change?
options: Magnesium sulfate is not a salt
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: Displacement needs a more reactive metal. A metal cannot be more reactive than itself.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: Metal X displaces copper from copper(II) sulfate but does not displace aluminium from aluminium sulfate. What could X be?
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: X lies between aluminium and copper, so zinc or iron fit.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: In 3Mg + 2Al³⁺ → 3Mg²⁺ + 2Al, which statement is correct?
options: Magnesium is the reducing agent because it donates electrons
Magnesium is reduced because it gains electrons
Al³⁺ is the reducing agent because it gains electrons
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: Magnesium loses electrons (is oxidised) and gives them to Al³⁺, so magnesium is the reducing agent.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: Which is the balanced equation for the thermite reaction?
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: 2Al + Fe₂O₃ → Al₂O₃ + 2Fe: two Al, two Fe and three O on each side.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: Why does aluminium displace iron from iron(III) oxide?
options: Iron is more reactive than aluminium
Aluminium is more reactive than iron
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: A more reactive metal takes the oxygen from the oxide of a less reactive metal.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: In the thermite reaction, which substance is reduced?
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: Iron(III) oxide loses oxygen, so it is reduced. 'Iron is reduced' loses the mark — name the oxide.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: What does 'exothermic' mean?
options: Heat is given out to the surroundings
Heat is taken in from the surroundings
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: Exothermic reactions give out heat (thermal energy). 'Energy released' on its own was ignored in 2024.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: Why does aluminium resist corrosion even though it is quite high in the reactivity series?
options: It is coated in a thin protective layer of aluminium oxide
It is always alloyed with zinc
It does not react with oxygen
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: The tough oxide layer stops water and oxygen reaching the metal underneath.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: Which property makes aluminium suitable for aircraft bodies?
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: Aluminium has a low density (and its alloys are strong and resist corrosion), so aircraft are lighter.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: Why is copper used for electrical wiring?
options: It has a low melting point
It is a very good electrical conductor and is ductile
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: Copper conducts electricity very well and can be drawn into wires.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: Why is copper used for water pipes?
options: It does not react with water
It is very hard and brittle
It dissolves slowly to clean the water
